Stroke (complications)

One 70-person post-stroke rehabilitation comparison reported less shoulder and hand pain, swelling and disability with laser therapy than electrotherapy. Improvement in independence was reported, but daily-activity results were not consistently superior.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

One 70-person post-stroke rehabilitation comparison reported less shoulder and hand pain, swelling and disability with laser therapy than electrotherapy. Improvement in independence was reported, but daily-activity results were not consistently superior.

Summary of the Evidence

The stroke-complications category contains one unique publication: a non-randomized clinical comparison in people with painful shoulder or shoulder-hand syndrome after stroke. It is a rehabilitation study of post-stroke complications, not an acute cerebral-stroke trial. No randomized PBM trial, independent replication, review, animal study or laboratory report was identified in this exact category.

Human and clinical evidence

Karabegović et al. compared laser therapy with electrotherapy in 70 post-stroke patients over a six-week treatment period. The authors reported greater reductions in pain, swelling and disability in the laser group and described improved independence. Daily-activity outcomes were not consistently superior, and the report provides limited detail on allocation methods and blinding (Karabegović et al. 2009). Exercise and ice massage were also part of rehabilitation care, so improvement cannot be attributed solely to laser treatment. This single comparison cannot establish a reliable treatment effect.

Animal evidence

No relevant animal study was identified in the post-stroke shoulder or hand-complication category.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone in-vitro or ex-vivo study was identified.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The study used an 830-nm near-infrared laser at 50 mW, with approximately 3 J per point reported in the database. Treatment was applied to the affected shoulder and hand over a schedule spanning six weeks. The comparison group received electrotherapy, and both groups continued rehabilitation. The local treatment and co-interventions are specific to post-stroke shoulder or hand symptoms and should not be generalized to acute stroke or neurological recovery more broadly.

Interpretation

The report supports a possible short-term reduction in pain and swelling in post-stroke shoulder-hand syndrome. Confidence is limited because it is one non-randomized comparison with co-interventions and incomplete information about bias control. The evidence does not establish durable improvement in independence or daily activity.

Evidence strength in source summaryLow for short-term pain and swelling reduction in post-stroke shoulder-hand syndrome because one non-randomized comparison favored laser therapy. Very low for sustained independence or daily activity.
Publications and records1 unique title

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The only publication compared laser treatment with electrotherapy in 70 post-stroke patients and reported less pain, swelling and disability in the laser group. Allocation and blinding were not adequately established, and both groups also received rehabilitation care. A concealed randomized trial with a sham and longer functional follow-up would support a stronger judgment.
